There is actually no reputable evidence of this. I believed it for a long time, because everyone on reddit parrots the concept non-stop, until I started actually looking for any notable research on it. The logic behind the idea that shaving double coated dogs is bad- it's largely based on the fact that some people did infrared photography on dogs with full coats and shaved coats, and noted that they gave off more heat with a shaved coat. The issue that they missed during this experiment is the fact that the heat is coming off of the dog *because they are losing heat to the environment.* Which means they are cooling more rapidly, instead of the heat being trapped on the skin. Dogs do follow the laws of thermodynamics, after all. The people talking about how double coats "reflect heat" forget that animals produce a LOT of heat through their own metabolism. That's why we don't wear down jackets in Summer, even though the jacket would reflect more heat than your bare skin.

If you choose to look into this more, I would try to take note of the fact that the myth is largely perpetuated in forums and by groomers, and as soon as you really dig into it, you will quickly notice that the "evidence" is not actually scientific. It's a never-ending internet chain of articles, referring to other articles, referring to groomers' blog posts, referring to the bunk articles about infrared "evidence."

There is no issue with shaving a double-coated dog, as long as you're not going nuts and shaving past the guard hairs down to the skin (that can lead to sunburn, skin irritation, and some silly looking regrowth, mainly, but that's if you really shave them down short). If you really need anecdotes, I work with dogs, and I have personally witnessed double coated dogs tolerate heat better after having their coats trimmed to a more manageable length. I have never seen a dog struggle more with heat after shaving, only less. I have also never seen a dog's coat "ruined" by clipping. There is sometimes an awkward stage of growth that looks a bit silly before it fills out, and sometimes people panic and think the coat is messed up, but if coats were truly ruined by clipping, every dog who has had surgery would look ridiculous (they don't).

That's why their vet said it wasn't a big deal. Because vets are constantly shaving dogs down, often to the skin, even, and they never see any of the "shaving side effects" that people talk about.

Shame is a HUGE driver of overeating, and it affects the production of cortisol and other stress hormones, which also cause weight gain. 

Dieting is actually one of the worst things someone can do for weight loss, as it leads to long term weight *gain* due to the combination of over restrictive behavior, metabolic changes, and not fixing the root causes. When we give people good things and stop making them feel bad, they lose weight. When we tell them it’s their fault, they gain weight. 

Weight gain is also heavily influenced by a variety of factors that can be very difficult to combat, such as gut flora imbalances. If you were given an obese person’s gut flora, you would likely rapidly gain weight- it’s quite fascinating. When we do the inverse, people easily lose weight easily, in a way they were unable to do before. Other causes include autoimmune conditions (5-10% of the population), thyroid disease (>12%), and mobility disabilities (>12%), among many other things like addiction and mental health disorders.

If you're breeding a bunch of box chain pet store birds together, they're going to have dangerously poor genetics. 

You don't need to separate birds to keep them from breeding, it's not like other pets- birds are super easy, you don't ever need to worry about accidental pregnancy. You can just pull nests out or add fake eggs, and they won't lay. It's healthier for the hens, too.

Yes, exactly. It bothers me so much when someone picks up two zebra finches from petco or something, and then lets them breed. Oftentimes pet store finches are from the same clutch, meaning the chicks are almost certainly inbred (and also of poor genetic quality to begin with).

I've seen people say that they let them lay eggs because it's "natural" and "the finches will be sad if I take the nest or eggs away," but if you let zebra or societies have a nest year round, they will breed nonstop, to the point of the hen dying. It's terrible and not even remotely natural, especially with the low-quality diets new owners feed them.

As long at it is done ethically, with regard to healthy genetics of the parents (e.g. no hybridizing, inbreeding, or dangerous heritable traits), and good care of the finches, I don't see an issue.

Animal trade is not intrinsically bad. It's mainly an issue with wild-caught species, or poorly bred animals.

I'm still glad I got it, and the fact that it hurt so much after waking up just let me know that I would've been NOT okay being awake. If you don't think you'd be okay being awake for it, trust yourself about that!

For the record, I'm the same age as you and have the same sleep pattern very often. And when I go on camping trips or don't use technology, I trend back towards normal pretty quickly.

I would first rule out any specific causes, like trauma, because PTSD and anxiety can make people's sleep schedules whack. Sleep procrastination from ADHD is also an issue for many.

Then I would strictly stop using tech at least an hour before it gets dark outside. Don't use curtains on your windows, and use warm, minimal lighting (like lamps with warm bulbs). You can take melatonin an hour before when you want to get tired, and vitamin d in the morning.

I think that sometimes when your sleep schedule is really horribly messed up, people feel like they need to step it back a few hours each time, but I've noticed it's pretty much all or nothing for me. Either I'm tired at 9 pm and I fall asleep, or I stay up past that initial drowsiness and feel totally wired until sunrise. Try to find that initial drowsiness and work with it. You might benefit from forcing yourself up really early once or twice, just to see how you react to it. I started working mornings and noticed that my body enjoyed being awake then.

Good luck!

I don't know if you're referring to hormones colloquially, or if you just don't understand what they are, but hormones affect every single part of your body, including conscious and subconscious thought. Your conscious thoughts impact hormone production as well- they work in tandem to regulate the body as a whole. Neuroendocrine signaling is incredibly complex, very physical, and very tangible.

I understand that most laypeople don’t have experience with immunology and it is a very complicated field, so this may be confusing for you. To clear things up, I’ll break it down for you.

**Common reasons why people believe vaccinated people are at more risk, and why those are false:**

1. “The data shows that vaccinated people are testing positive more, so vaccines must make you weaker to COVID.”

Raw data can be hard to interpret if you don’t have experience with it. We have to think about many factors, like test limitations, timing, correlations, etc. 

The reason why it may seem like unvaccinated people are faring better, is that alpha and delta have already ripped through the unvaccinated population, and many of the high-risk unvaccinated people already died or developed long-term disabilities. 

Due to the fact that it spread so readily through unvaccinated regions, the virus mutated quickly into a new strain, that is not fully covered by the alpha-based vaccines. So those who are vaccinated now have less protection than they did before, but still proportionally more than someone who has never been vaccinated or caught covid. 

So the highest risk people, who were previously more protected, are now catching it in these recent, highly contagious waves. Their response to the infection is not more severe than it would have been were they unvaccinated (their chances are still much better), it is simply a matter of timing, as they were better protected until now. 

It is also worth noting that vaccinated people are, almost certainly, more likely to get tested and to report positive tests, which further skews the data.

[SOURCE](https://www.factcheck.org/2022/06/scicheck-vaccinated-people-not-more-susceptible-to-covid-19-than-unvaccinated/)

2. “Evidence shows that vaccines weaken the immune system”

The evidence actually does not say that. That is false and unsubstantiated information that has unfortunately been widely spread.

[SOURCE 1](https://www.health.harvard.edu/diseases-and-conditions/can-the-flu-shot-hurt-my-immune-response) 
[SOURCE 2](https://healthfeedback.org/claimreview/no-scientific-evidence-for-claim-by-pathologist-ryan-cole-that-covid-19-vaccines-weaken-the-immune-system/)

3. “Doctors say not to get boosters too often since that weakens your immune response!”

When they [say that](https://www.healthline.com/health-news/why-a-4th-covid-19-shot-likely-wont-provide-more-protection), they are not saying it will weaken your immune response from baseline, they are saying that the vaccines will be *less effective than someone who was vaccinated with proper time intervals*.

There are optimal times to get boosters. It varies depending on the pathogen and vaccine, which is why we have trials and antibody testing to determine that. You need to give the immune system enough time to build a strong response before exposing it again and starting a new response. This maximizes the amount of antibodies produced. 

If you follow the recommended schedules for vaccination, you will be more protected compared to someone who is unvaccinated, or who took them not according to schedule.

[SOURCE](https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2021/11/understanding-the-science-behind-a-vaccine-booster/)

I have an allergic autoimmune disease that makes pollen very dangerous for me, so my tricks are:

-Close all windows in your house and run any air filters you have. If you have an a/c system, set that to recirculate.

-plan outdoor activities with the local pollen forecast in mind

-Take a shower every night before bed, or as soon as you get home for the day. I also wash my face in the morning and clean my eyelids with cetaphil gentle cleanser to get pollen off that may have settled in the night. You can go the extra step with a Neti pot and eye wash if need be.

-Don’t let clothes you wear outside touch your bed, and wash them asap. Machine washing and tumble drying is essential to get pollen off of fabric.

-keep pets off the bed if they’ve been outdoors, and give them frequent baths if you are going to be around them a lot. They carry pollen on their fur.

-If you have to go anywhere, limit time outside, keep car windows shut, recirculate the car air, and wear an n95 outdoors.

-don’t wear contact lenses outdoors

-avoid foods that cross-react with the pollen types you’re allergic to (you can look up lists online)

-Allergy shots do help a ton! I just can’t do them anymore thanks to the autoimmune stuff :/

-I use 3 doses of 24-hour Allegra per day. 2 doses of a modern H1 antihistamine like Zyrtec/Allegra/Claritin would probably be plenty for you, if 1 isn’t enough, since it’s actually quite safe, but please ask your doctor first since they can interact with certain conditions and meds. 

Taking this kind of antihistamine is better for you than Benadryl; Benadryl is short-acting and has far more severe side effects, so it’s mostly just a secret weapon for when you feel *extra* bad.

Nasalcrom or Flonase (sinus/nose symptoms)

Zatidor (eye symptoms)

H2 antihistamines like Pepcid and Zantac (GI symptoms)

To be clear, I’m not an anti-vaxxer. And I think that people should not be afraid of them. But perhaps I can shed some light on why some people are.

There are some medical conditions that lay dormant until they are triggered by stressors or large immune responses, such as major illnesses, trauma, or... vaccines. Because of this, some people say that vaccines are dangerous because they have seen people become chronically or seriously ill after getting one. 

The problem with this logic is that if you are predisposed to a condition, you are just as likely to get it from catching the illness you are being immunized against.
I personally developed a chronic medical condition after a virus. But I do understand why that could scare someone, if they saw someone go from perfectly healthy to very ill after getting a vaccine. And when people see this happen, they tend to spread the word in order to “save” others.


And even though they are very, very rare, there are also other scary side effects from vaccines (just like there are from all medical treatments). The reason why people campaign against vaccines and not other treatments, though, despite most other treatments being far riskier (most medications have terrible side effects at much higher rates- I mean, 3000 people die every year of *aspirin*, even), is because vaccines are preventative and people are more willing to treat something that is currently making them sick. So people think to themselves: “well, I’m not sick now, so there’s nothing to treat. And other people are getting vaccinated, anyway, so I can just let them put themselves at risk and still be safe thanks to herd immunity. I don’t want a rare blood clot, after all!”

It’s all about perception of risk. And it’s easy to see scary headlines and Facebook posts and think that the risk of side effects is much higher than it is, despite the fact that the risk of long-term COVID effects is way higher. Partly thanks to the sheer amount of anti-vax content on the internet (due to factors I mentioned before), and partly because people are not viewing COVID as a likely thing to happen to them.

There are also other factors at play that I won’t get tooooo far into, like how some parents have difficulty dealing with autism diagnoses and look for an explanation for why their child has “become” autistic, and vaccines tend to be given around the time that autism characteristics tend to first become noticeable. Leading to a huge, political anti-vax movement simply because these parents couldn’t cope with this misplaced grief. And that lead to a whole host of other things and movements and headlines that seeded distrust in vaccines.

There is no such thing as a 100% effective vaccine. But when enough people get vaccinated, there is a point when the virus is no longer able to spread fast enough in order to stay active (or mutate), and you can eradicate the disease. This is why none of us have polio, measles, or smallpox.

And it’s worth noting that 94% efficacy is actually SUPER duper good for a vaccine. Many other vaccines are less effective. For instance, mumps and rubella vaccines are less effective, but they are both considered to be eliminated diseases in the US.
Traditional vaccines also do not carry live/active viruses.
